 Live .  2,976 viewing 2976 viewing Live page Updated 2 minutes ago Trump meets Modi and other world leaders in Philippines on first leg of Asia trip
 Summary
 Donald Trump is in the Philippines on the first leg of a high-profile trip to Asia - images show the US president meeting India's Narendra Modi, Australia's Anthony Albanese and Japan's Sanae Takaichi
 "We have a great relationship with these people and these countries," Trump tells reporters , adding Modi is a "very tough man" and Takaichi "may be even tougher"
 Earlier, a red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he touched down at an airport in the Philippine capital, Manila 
 Trump walked down the steps of Air Force One and was greeted by a band playing YMCA, writes our South East Asia correspondent 
 After his overnight stay in Manila, Trump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin

 Edited by Manish Pandey, with reporting from Jonathan Head in Manila and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
 'If it's available, I would': Trump on meeting Putin published at 11:21 GMT 11:21 GMT 
 President Trump has also been asked about the possibility of a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, to which he replies he doesn't know if that will happen.
 "If it's available, I would," he adds.
 The US president tells the assembled media that Putin is coming to China, and Trump too is "the guest of President Xi". 
 He is also asked if North Korean leader Kim Jong Un will be there, to which Trump replies by saying "he would like too, we'll see what happens". 
 Trump adds he will press President Xi Jinping and President Putin on the Iran war, "to get involved, to get it ended".

 Trump and Modi's relationship has soured over the last year published at 11:05 GMT 11:05 GMT 
 Cherylann Mollan 
Reporting from Mumbai 
 In comments to reporters, Trump has just described Indian PM Narendra Modi as a "tough man". 
 While Modi is meeting Trump along with other leaders of the Quad - a separate bilateral meet looks unlikely. 
 It's the first time the pair have met since June when they briefly met on the sidelines of the G7 summit in Paris. The one today comes against the backdrop of prolonged negotiations over a US-India trade deal, but no updates around it are expected to come out of their meeting in Manila.
 Analysts will also be closely watching the body language of the two leaders. Trump and Modi shared a warm relationship during the US president’s first term and even made joint appearances at massive rallies in Houston and Ahmedabad. 
 Modi was one of the first world leaders to visit Trump at the White House last year after he was sworn in. But since then, the relationship has soured, with Trump slapping high tariffs on India, and putting Delhi in a tight spot with comments he made on the country’s conflict with Pakistan.
 The two leaders have spoken on the phone several times since then, and Indian ministers have indicated the trade deal negotiations are progressing. But it will be interesting to see whether they look as comfortable as they did earlier.

 Modi is 'a very tough man', says Trump ahead of meeting published at 11:02 GMT 11:02 GMT 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, (L-R) Narendra Modi, Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese
 Trump has also been taking questions during the photographs.
 Asked about the plan for his meeting with the leaders of Japan, India and Australia, Donald Trump says: "We have a great relationship with these people and these countries."
 "We have right from the beginning... they're friends of mine so that helps."
 Gesturing at Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Trump says "he's a very tough man, and she [Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi] may be even tougher".
 Turning to Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Trump adds: "And we... we're okay".

 Trump meets Japan, Australia and India leaders published at 10:49 GMT 10:49 GMT Breaking 
 Image source, Reuters It's been a quick turnaround for Donald Trump, who touched down in Manila a short while ago and has headed to meet the leaders of Australia, Japan, and India - known as the "Quad". 
 Following their photo together, Trump, Narendra Modi, Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi will have a quadrilateral summit.

 What you need to know about the Quad alliance published at 10:35 GMT 10:35 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Quad last met in 2024 when Joe Biden was US president. (L-R) Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Joe Bidenm and former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida
 Donald Trump is attending the first Quad meeting in two years. The group last gathered in 2024 in Delaware during the presidency Joe Biden. Here is what you need to know about the alliance.
 Who is in the Quad? The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue brings together the US, Japan, Australia and India. It began as a loose grouping to provide aid following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and was relaunched in 2017.
 What are its aims? With its focus on the Indo-Pacific, the Quad says it backs the free and open, rules-based global order - its unstated goal is containing an increasingly assertive China in its backyard. Member nations' ties with China have deteriorated in recent years.
 What's at stake? The US must persuade its allies - united by concern at China's rise but differing on other issues - that it's committed to a region seen as key to global security and prosperity. China says the region should beware what it calls the "Asian Nato".

 Trump's first order of business: The Quad meeting published at 10:14 GMT 10:14 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, reporting from Manila 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Foreign ministers from the Quad meet on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta in October
 President Trump’s first meeting at the Asean summit will be with America's partners in the Quad - India, Japan and Australia.
 But 19 years after it was first proposed by then Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, and then relaunched by none other than President Trump on his first visit as president to Asia in 2017, what has the Quad really achieved?
 Intended as a strategic counterweight to China’s relentlessly rising influence in Asia, it risks being seen as little more than a talking shop and empty symbol of co-operation - very much the kind of criticism often levelled at Asean.

 Filipino president's son to greet Trump published at 09:55 GMT 09:55 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, reporting from Manila 
 The helicopter Marine One is on the tarmac waiting to take President Trump on the short flight to the Solaire Hotel where he will spend most of his brief visit to Manila.
 The government has laid on a troupe of young dancers in traditional dress and a military band in 19th Century uniform. Last year Trump amused everyone on arriving in Kuala Lumpur by dancing along with the welcoming troupe.
 Son of the Philippines president, Sandro, a congressman, is there to greet Trump.

 President Trump flew to Manila in his new plane gifted by Qatar published at 09:44 GMT 09:44 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, reporting from Manila 
 President Trump has landed in Manila travelling on the Boeing 747 gifted to him by Qatar. 
 Some regions of the world are considered unsuitable for the new plane, which does not have the levels of defences on the existing presidential 747. 
 Presumably, the Asia-Pacific region was considered safe enough.

 What's been happening today at the summit? published at 09:26 GMT 09:26 GMT 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images It's late in the afternoon in the Philippines, and it's been a busy day as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) wraps up its annual summit. 
 The 11 Asean member states held summits with China, Japan, India and other regional partners.
 President Trump is expected to touch down in the Filipino capital shortly, and later he'll meet with South East Asian leaders and America's "Quad" security allies - Japan, Australia and India.
 Happening alongside this is the summit's closing ceremony.
 Trump's arrival is expected after the conclusion of this ceremony which will see the Philippines hand chairmanship of Asean over to Singapore. The regional bloc rotate chair every year.

 The Asean summit has been going on for days before Trump's arrival published at 09:15 GMT 09:15 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, reporting from Manila 
 When President Trump arrives in Manila at the very end of this year’s Asean summit, he will inevitably suck all the oxygen out of the room.
 But it's worth remembering this summit has been going on for three days, and has been attended by South East Asian heads of government - with the exception of Myanmar, which is still being kept at arms length - and other world leaders from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, Brazil. 
 It is almost as if to get in one last word before the Trump wagon train rolls in.
 Chinese Premier Li Qiang extolled the "extraordinary achievements" of the Asean-China partnership at a time of rising protectionisms and unilateralism.
 China-Asean trade now exceeds $1 trillion (£760bn), well ahead of the $686 billion in US-Asean trade last year, despite that growing 20% over 2024 on the back of soaring demand for tech components.

 What is Asean? published at 09:09 GMT 09:09 GMT 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) is a regional bloc, formed in the 1960s to promote economic and political cooperation in South East Asia.
 But unlike other regional organisations like the European Union, which enforce binding laws on its members, Asean's decision-making processes are based on principles of non-interference and consensus. 
 It's a format that has suited the region's diversity and at times conflicting political interests.
 Twice a year, South East Asia's leaders gather at the Asean summit. The meeting is held in the country holding the Asean chairmanship, a title that is rotated annually among the 11 member states.
 The Philippines is this year's chairman.

 Protests await Trump in Manila published at 09:04 GMT 09:04 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Filipinos felt the pain when the Iran war pushed oil prices through the roof. The country imports 98% of its oil from the Gulf. 
 The Philippines became the first country in the world to declare a national emergency because of the rise in oil prices. Inflation soared, worsening the country's economic slump.
 Protesters will take to the streets in Manila to show the US president their frustration. 
 They will also be voicing their opposition to the Philippines joining the US-led AI initiative Pax Silica - which the State Department says is about advancing a "new economic security consensus among allies and trusted partners".
 Many Filipionos fear building data centres in farm lands north of the capital will guzzle up millions of gallons of water and displace farmers and indigenous tribes.

 Trump to touch down in the Philippines shortly published at 09:01 GMT 09:01 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The US president boarding Air Force One in Maryland on Monday
 It's just gone 17:00 local time (09:00 GMT) in Manila, as President Trump is shortly expected to arrive in the Philippines, kicking off the first leg of an Asia trip which will take him to China on Wednesday for an expected meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
 Trump’s visit to the capital comes at the end of the annual summit of South East Asian leaders - Asean - often attended by US presidents.
 Here he is scheduled to hold a series of meetings focused on regional security, trade and American supply chain concerns at a time when US commitment to its Asian allies has been called into question.
 Among those is a meeting with US partners in the Quad security alliance - Japan, Australia and India. Xi had earlier criticised the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing.
 There is a lot of ground to cover as Trump journeys across East Asia. 
 Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates and analysis from our correspondents on the ground.
